title: Fitting a plastic rodding eye to a soil pipe
subtitle: Cut into a plastic soil stack and fit a rodding access eye so the discharge pipe can be cleared without dismantling fittings
excerpt: How to fit a plastic rodding eye to an existing plastic soil pipe stack or horizontal branch. Covers marking and cutting the pipe, fitting a slip coupling or strap boss with a rodding cap, and testing the seal.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK plastic pipework manufacturers' installation guidance (open access). Building Regulations Approved Document H on drainage.

glossaryTerms.definition: A capped access fitting installed into a drain or soil pipe, sealed with a screw or push-fit cover when not in use. When the cover is removed, drain rods or a jetting nozzle can be inserted to clear a blockage without dismantling the pipework.

A plastic fitting that clamps around the outside of a soil pipe and includes a spigot for a branch connection or an access eye. Fitted without cutting the main pipe: a hole is drilled through the strap boss into the pipe. Used for adding a branch connection or a rodding point to an existing run.

content.text: gives permanent access to a soil stack or underground branch for clearing blockages. The most practical method is a
fitted over the existing pipe: clamp, drill, cap. No pipe cutting needed.

Fit the rodding eye above where a branch joins the stack, or at a bend. The rod needs to reach the most likely blockage. Keep the access cap clear. Do not put it inside a sealed boxing unless the boxing has a removable panel.

Clean the pipe at the boss location. Put solvent cement on the seal. Clamp the boss to the pipe and tighten the screws. Drill through the boss and pipe with a hole saw sized to match the spigot. Fish out or catch the cut plug so it does not fall into the drain.
Fit the rodding cap and seal

Fit the rodding cap onto the strap boss spigot. Most rodding caps are screw-fit: tighten by hand, then a quarter-turn with a large screwdriver or water-pump pliers. The cap seal must be watertight but not so tight that it cannot be removed in future. Check the seal by running water from a tap into the stack above the boss and watching for any drip from the cap joint.

attrs.symptom: Sewage smell from around the rodding cap after fitting
attrs.cause: The cap seal is not fully tight or the rubber seal inside the boss is not seated correctly.
attrs.fix: Remove the cap, check the rubber seal is in its groove, apply fresh plumber's grease to the thread, and refit the cap finger-tight plus a quarter-turn.

attrs.symptom: The drilled plug falls into the soil pipe during drilling
attrs.cause: The hole saw was not held at the correct angle, or the plug was not caught before it dropped.
attrs.fix: Try to retrieve the plug with a retrieval hook or drain rods before it reaches the trap. If it reaches the underground drain, rod from the nearest inspection chamber.
